Why a birth should defile at all two of them answer the same way, and one makes it an argument against a named heretic. Calvin says the ceremony reminded the Jews of the common corruption of our nature, since the whole race of Adam is polluted, so the woman contracts uncleanness from the offspring she bears and is further contaminated by giving it birth; hence it appears how foul our condition is in God's sight, since at our birth, and before it, we infect our mothers. He corrects what he calls an almost universal but very absurd reading, that what is condemned is libidinous intercourse, since the purification is not required unless there be offspring, so the impurity charged is not in the intercourse but in the generation. From this he refutes Pelagius, who denied that Adam's sin was propagated among his descendants and held that we contract sin by imitation and not by origin: the mother would not be unclean if the children were pure. And he guards marriage from the inference: if the marriage couch is free from stain that is due to God's indulgence, its sanctity covering what might otherwise be imputed as blame. Henry reaches the same doctrine by a shorter road, that this uncleanness signified the pollution of sin we are all conceived and born in, for if the root be impure so is the branch; and the mother's exclusion from the sanctuary signified that our original corruption would have shut us out for ever from God had he not provided for our purifying.

Why the term is doubled for a daughter is the real question, and Calvin canvasses four answers before choosing. Some ascribe it to a natural cause; he grants that continence was part of the intention but says the ceremony's object was different. He reports the view that the mother is more defiled by female offspring because that sex is more disposed to vice, and says he knows not whether it is sound. He thinks it more probable, as some hold, that the woman was the beginning of the rebellion, being deceived by the serpent and drawing husband and posterity into the same ruin. But it seems more correct to him that the punishment for males was lightened by circumcision, since although God consecrated both sexes in that symbol he honoured males by engraving his covenant on their flesh. Henry refuses to guess: why the time should be double for a female he can assign no reason but the will of the Law-maker, adding that in Christ Jesus no difference is made of male and female. Ellicott gives the historical answer, that the ancients believed the derangement of the system far greater at the birth of a girl, and shows the belief was not peculiar to this law: the Greeks held that a man who had been near a woman in childbirth defiled the altar, one measure for purifying an island in their great war was to forbid women to be confined there, the Hindoos count a newborn's relations impure, and among the Arabs the mother remains unclean forty days.

On the eighth day for circumcision the reasons divide. Gill and Ellicott make it depend on the mother, whose stricter period of uncleanness ends then, so she no longer imparts defilement by touch; Henry says the same, that the males shared her pollution during the days of separation. Clarke gives a physical reason, that before this the child could scarcely have strength to bear the operation, and after it there was no need to delay, since until the rite was performed the child was not reckoned in covenant with God. Ellicott alone notices what the law omits, since it legislates only for ordinary cases and passes over twins, so the administrators under the second Temple had to supplement it, ruling that a mother of twins of both sexes kept the longer term.

Coming to the offerings, Clarke pauses to reject two explanations of the doubled term. It is not easy, he says, to account for the difference at all: there is probably no physical reason for it and difficult to assign a political one. Some of the ancient physicians assert that a woman is in the order of nature much longer in completely recovering after the birth of a female, and he answers that this assertion is justified neither by observation nor by matter of fact. Others think the difference intended to mark the inferiority of the female sex, and he calls that a miserable reason, pitifully supported. Two of the others settle a smaller point instead. Keil insists that the purification was for the woman herself and not for the child, since it was the woman who was unclean and not the infant to which she had given birth; Ellicott says the same, that the phrase means with regard to a son or a daughter, according to which she had borne. And Gill and Ellicott agree on the day, that the offerings were brought not on the fortieth or the eightieth but on the day after, the ancient rule being that a new mother waits until her sun is set and brings her offering on the morrow.

Why the lamb should be named before the bird two of them notice, since the usual order is the reverse. Gill reports the rule as a Jewish commentator gives it, that in oblations the sacrifice for sin goes first, guilt being expiated so that the gift may be accepted, and confesses that here the order is inverted and the reason not very apparent. Ellicott supplies one: precedence goes to whichever victim is the costlier. On what each was for, Henry takes the first as thankfulness for a safe deliverance and hope of further favour to mother and child, since where there is joy there must be thanks and where there is hope there must be prayer; and he notes that the expiatory victim was identical for rich and poor, for whatever difference of means appears in the gifts of acknowledgment, the price of atonement is one. He allows two accounts of what it covered: the completing of a ceremonial defilement that merely figured moral pollution, or a real fault, whether an inordinate longing after children or impatience under the pangs of travail. Ellicott reports the second from the ancients, who made the one gift confess reproachful thoughts harboured before the birth and the other expiate words heedlessly spoken in the hour of anguish.

The provision for the poor is where all of them end, and they end in the same place. Ellicott calls it a merciful indulgence, adds that the pair must be of one kind and not one of each, and observes that this was what the mother of our Lord presented at the Temple. Gill draws from it the state of poverty she was in, and takes her circumcising of the child and her purification together as showing that both were under the law and obedient to it. Henry says the same and presses it, that Christ's parents were so poor they could not bring a lamb, and that he was so early made under the law in order to redeem those that were under it. Clarke turns it into an exclamation: the only heir to the throne of David was not able to bring a lamb to offer in sacrifice to God, and how abominable must sin be when it required him who was in the form of God thus to empty himself.
